job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

response.passage: Many students think that if a material comes from a plant, it must be completely natural. For example, Rayon is made from wood pulp, but it is actually called a semi-synthetic fibre because it undergoes extensive chemical treatment. Unlike natural cotton, Rayon is modified in factories. Another common myth is that a polymer is just one giant atom. In reality, a polymer is a very large unit formed by joining thousands of small repeating chemical units called monomers. When comparing strength, people often assume natural silk is the strongest. However, a synthetic nylon thread is actually stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness. While these fibres are useful, we must handle plastics carefully. Some believe all plastics melt when heated. This is only true for thermoplastics. Thermosetting plastics, like Bakelite used in electrical switches, do not soften or melt once they are moulded, even if heated again. Finally, we must manage waste wisely. Some think burning plastic makes it disappear, but it actually releases poisonous fumes into the atmosphere. Burying it doesn't help either, as plastic is non-biodegradable and won't turn into compost even after hundreds of years. We must follow the 5R principle—Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover, and Refuse—to protect our environment.
response.summary: Rayon is a semi-synthetic fibre created through chemical processing, and polymers are large structures made of repeating units rather than single atoms. While synthetic fibres like nylon offer great strength, plastics require careful disposal because they are non-biodegradable and release toxins when burned.
